public_rationale: The July 2026 study supports the proposed capability through simulated web-comment injection, realistic data filtering, and controlled training tests. It addresses training contamination directly. The adverse audit of a particular propaganda campaign limits claims about observed deployment, but does not negate this capability.
limitations: The decisive study is a preprint using sandboxed injections and models up to 1.3 billion parameters.
It does not document a successful live attack against a deployed frontier model.
Instruction tuning reduced some effects; ingestion and success depend on the pipeline and content.
Experimental execution dates were not specified; event dates use the reported study year.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: If swarms flood the web with duplicative, crawler-targeted content, they can execute 'LLM grooming', poisoning the training data that future AI models (and citizens) rely on.
conditions: swarms flood the web with duplicative, crawler-targeted content

statement.excerpt: If swarms flood the web with duplicative, crawler-targeted content, they can execute “LLM grooming,” poisoning the training data that future AI models (and citizens) rely on.
statement.document_title: AI bot swarms threaten to undermine democracy

our_interpretation: This is a conditional capability claim, not a forecast that a particular campaign will succeed.
The ordinary reading is that coordinated publication of repeated malicious narratives can contaminate subsequently collected training data and affect model behavior.
‘Duplicative’ permits repeated narratives with wording variations; it does not require every document to be byte-identical.
The parenthetical reference to citizens describes downstream reliance on information. It does not specify a measurable human persuasion effect.
criteria.support_condition: Experiments or traced campaigns establish a feasible route from crawler-targeted web publication through training-data collection and filtering to changed trained-model behavior.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence establishes that the proposed publication route cannot produce training contamination or behavioral effects under representative conditions. Failure of one campaign alone does not disprove a capability claim.

evidence.publisher: arXiv; University of Washington and Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence researchers
evidence.explanation: Sandboxed comment injection and crawl-data analysis establish a feasible path through extraction and filtering. Separate controlled training experiments find shifts toward attacker-preferred answers, including with less conspicuous repeated content.

Supports susceptibility once malicious documents enter training. It tests a gibberish-producing backdoor and directly inserts documents, so it alone would not establish the claimed web-publication pathway.

evidence.excerpt: little evidence to support the grooming theory.
evidence.explanation: This audit found limited evidence for successful grooming in a specific Kremlin-disinformation case. It cautions against claiming documented real-world success, but does not disprove the experimental capability.
